title: Railway time
bodyMd:
Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every town kept its own time, set by the sun: noon was the moment the sun stood highest over that town. Because the sun's position shifts as one travels east or west, the clocks of two towns a hundred kilometres apart could differ by several minutes. For most of history the difference did not matter, since nobody travelled fast enough to notice it.

Railways changed that. A timetable that listed departures in the local time of each station was confusing to passengers and, more seriously, dangerous to operate on single-track lines, where two trains travelling towards each other had to be kept apart by the timetable alone. Railway companies responded by running their trains on a single reference time, usually that of the capital or of the company's headquarters, and displaying it on station clocks, sometimes alongside the local time.

What followed is often told as a story of efficiency defeating tradition, but the record is more mixed. In many towns the two times coexisted for decades. Churches and town halls kept local time, the station kept railway time, and residents learned to ask which was meant. Legal adoption of a single national time frequently came long after railways had made it the practical standard, and in some places it was prompted less by trains than by disputes over when contracts expired or when polling stations closed.

The episode is a reminder that a technical standard can become dominant without being imposed. Railway time spread because those who most needed precise coordination adopted it first, and others found it convenient to follow; the law, when it arrived, often recorded a change that had already happened.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage, with no figure or table, about the spread of railway time in the nineteenth century. Towns once kept local solar time, differing by minutes. Railways found local times confusing and, on single-track lines where opposing trains were separated only by the timetable, dangerous, so they ran on one reference time shown on station clocks, sometimes beside local time. The third paragraph says the common story of efficiency defeating tradition is too simple: the two times coexisted for decades, and laws adopting national time often came later, sometimes prompted by disputes over contracts or polling hours. The last paragraph says a standard can become dominant without being imposed, with the law often recording a change that had already happened.
